Volga pikeperch (Sander volgensis) attains an ultimate total length of 45 cm [Li = 45 cm], a size that distinguishes it from its larger congener, Sander lucioperca, and reflects its adaptation to middle and lower river reaches of the Ponto-Caspian basin. Females typically reach puberty at a total length of 25 cm [Lp = 25 cm], with a range of 20 to 30 cm reported across different populations; this relatively early onset of maturation is common among medium-sized percids that experience moderate predation pressure. Under controlled laboratory conditions at a water temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) was measured at 7.74% [GSI = 7.74%].

Embryonic development proceeds relatively quickly at the thermal regime typical of this species' spring spawning habitat. Eggs incubated at 16 °C [T = 16 °C] complete embryogenesis and the yolk-sac larva emerges after approximately 15 days [ab = approximately 15 days], a period consistent with the incubation durations observed in other temperate sander species. The wet weight at birth, calculated from the average egg diameter of 0.9 mm typical of the genus, is approximately 0.00038 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00038 grams]. This extremely small initial mass places the newly hatched prolarva among the smallest percid larvae relative to adult size, a pattern that necessitates a rich supply of zooplankton during the critical transition from endotrophic to exogenous feeding. The timing of exogenous feeding onset is tightly coupled to the complete resorption of the yolk sac, which typically occurs within a few days following eclosion.

Growth from the larval stage through the juvenile recruitment phase is rapid under optimal thermal conditions. Field studies indicate that sexual maturation, defined by the onset of vitellogenesis in females, occurs when individuals reach a wet weight of approximately 176 grams [Wwp = approximately 176 grams], corresponding to the previously described length at puberty of 25 cm. This marked investment in somatic growth before reproductive activation reflects a life-history trade-off common among iteroparous freshwater teleosts, wherein deferring reproduction until a larger body size is achieved confers higher fecundity and greater competitive ability at spawning sites. The maximum recorded wet weight for adult Sander volgensis in productive river reaches is approximately 1080 grams [Wwi = approximately 1080 grams], though individuals exceeding 1000 grams are encountered only in populations with abundant forage fish and low fishing mortality.

Maximum lifespan estimates for the Volga pikeperch, based on otolith annuli from populations inhabiting thermally stable reservoirs at 16 °C [T = 16 °C], indicate that the oldest documented individuals reach approximately 12 years [am = approximately 12 years]. This longevity is intermediate among European percids, falling between the shorter-lived Eurasian ruffe and the longer-lived zander, and likely reflects a combination of moderate metabolic rate and relatively low natural predation on adults. Reproductive senescence has not been systematically investigated in this species, but the presence of 10- and 11-year-old gravid females in museum collections suggests that fecundity is maintained well into advanced age. The 12-year maximum lifespan (approximately 12 years) [am = approximately 12 years] is notable given the species' somewhat compressed growing season in its native range, which spans latitudes from the lower Volga through the Don and Dnieper river systems at a temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C].

The Volga pikeperch is typically found in the middle and lower reaches of large rivers with moderate flow and high turbidity, where it occupies deep channel habitats during the day and moves into shallow foraging areas at dusk. Its diet shifts ontogenetically from zooplankton and small benthic invertebrates during the larval and juvenile stages to predominantly fish prey, including small cyprinids and gobiids, once adults surpass approximately 25 cm in length. This piscivorous habit, combined with a relatively low metabolic demand at the thermal regime of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], allows the species to maintain stable populations even in systems with moderate productivity, and its life history position between earlier-maturing, smaller percids and larger, longer-lived ones underscores its ecological specialization within European freshwater fish communities.
